abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: A systematic, PRISMA‐guided review led by our consortium screened 23,781 human microbiome papers and procured 2896 studies published from 2012 to 2025 that were then scored by reviewers into four Biological Host‐Associated AI‐Ready Metadata (BHAM) tiers. Only 5.9% of studies deposited sequence data with per‐sample host disease status, age, and sex, and 63.1% shared no reusable sequence data, so that 85.5% of roughly 720,000 samples cannot be reused for cross‐cohort or artificial intelligence (AI) analyses without contacting the authors. Sequence deposition improved modestly over time, whereas per‐sample annotation did not. Journals, repositories, and researchers should require structured, machine‐readable metadata at submission, supported by AI‐assisted curation.

sec.p: Revised 2026 Oct 28; Received 2026 Sep 16; Accepted 2026 Oct 31.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly being adopted in biology. In the last 2 years, biological foundation models, including DNA language models such as Evo 2 [1], have moved from proof‐of‐concept to routine tools for prediction and design across proteins, genomes, and cells. Each successive generation has required an order‐of‐magnitude increase in training data [2]. This has been feasible largely because DNA sequence deposition is required by journal and funding agency mandates, ensuring access to a large amount of public genomic data for training purposes.

Microbiome science could follow a similar trajectory, but while large‐scale analyses exist [3], leveraging the entirety of public microbiome data remains a challenge. The first few microbiome foundation models suggest that self‐supervised learning across aggregated cohorts can yield transferable disease representations [4, 5, 6]. However, the microbiome field lacks an equivalent, centralized, AI‐ready resource that leverages all public data, blocking comparable model training efforts.

This gap is driven by what we deem a major roadblock in data reuse, in which the DNA sequence data are available, but the information about the biospecimens, subjects, sampling locations, and other aspects of the study required to interpret the sequence data are absent. The International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC), which consists of the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Sequence Read Archive (SRA), the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA), and the DNA Data Bank of Japan (DDBJ), provides infrastructure for raw data preservation and synchronizes records across archives [7]. While these repositories have required metadata fields that authors must fill it out, it is often the custom metadata attributes that carry most of the biological signal, including disease status, treatment, clinical phenotype, diet, and medication. Thus, true data reuse has largely become an honor system, reliant on authors taking the time to upload complete metadata.

Standards such as the Genomic Standards Consortium's Minimum Information about any (x) Sequence (MIxS), and reporting guidelines such as the Strengthening The Organization and Reporting of Microbiome Studies (STORMS), and its environmental equivalent, the Standards for Technical Reporting in Environmental and host‐Associated Microbiome Studies (STREAMS), aim to improve consistency [8, 9, 10], yet adoption rates are unclear. Data reuse practices continue to reflect older frameworks such as the Bermuda Principles, which predate large‐scale multi‐omics integration [11]. These limitations contribute to persistent gaps in FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) compliance [12]. Building on top of FAIR principles, AI‐ready data are structured, machine‐actionable, and harmonized at the per‐sample level (e.g., standardized host disease, age, and sex fields) so that they can be ingested directly into large‐scale models without manual curation or author contact. Thus, a fair degree of overlap exists between FAIR and AI‐ready principles.

Large‐scale curation efforts, such as Metalog [13] and Meta2DB [14], highlight the challenge in aggregating public microbiome data with proper metadata. Both databases aggregate tens of thousands of samples but are still limited to studies that were properly annotated in repositories. Emerging frameworks such as the Searchable, Planetary‐scale mIcrobiome REsource (SPIRE) and Data Reuse Information (DRI) tags provide partial solutions but lack broad adoption [11]. A complementary recent effort [15] introduced a tier‐based FAIR badge system and automated checker for microbiome publications, underscoring growing concern about reusability. However, a comprehensive manually curated effort that assesses microbiome data reusability with both human health and AI‐guided large‐scale meta‐analysis in mind, is lacking.

Here, we provide a new reusability‐tiered system we call Biological Host‐Associated AI‐Ready Metadata (BHAM; Figure 1), specifically targeted metadata variables that require sample‐level annotations for health‐oriented human microbiome studies. We conducted an unprecedented audit of reusability in the clinical human microbiome literature and identified major reusability gaps that the community needs to address.

caption.p: Reusability tiers for human microbiome sequence data and metadata. The Biological Host‐Associated AI‐Ready Metadata (BHAM) framework classifies each study by what its repository deposit allows a reader to reuse without contacting the authors. Tier 1, per‐sample host disease status, age, and sex are recorded in the repository; Tier 2, per‐sample disease status is recoverable from a metadata field or an informative sample name; Tier 3, sequence data are accessible with unique sample identifiers but no per‐sample host metadata; Tier 4, no accessible or valid accession, or no sample‐level identifiers. Percentages give the share of the 2896 analyzed studies in each tier. AI, artificial intelligence; BHAM, Biological Host‐Associated AI‐Ready Metadata; DDBJ, DNA Data Bank of Japan; ENA, European Nucleotide Archive; SRA, Sequence Read Archive.

sec.title: MOST HUMAN MICROBIOME STUDIES LACK REUSABLE PER‐SAMPLE METADATA
sec.p: To quantify the impact of these limitations, we manually screened 23,781 articles following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Figure S1; see Methods in the Supporting Information), to procure 2896 human microbiome publications that involved DNA sequencing. Our resulting dataset consisted of articles from 2012 to 2025, spanning more than 50 countries, 6 continents, and a range of host body sites and disease groups (Figure S2; Tables S1 and S2). We constructed this dataset through a systematic search of PubMed, covering human microbiome studies across major diseases of interest. Each study was assessed against three reusability criteria, namely the presence of a public accession code, availability of sample‐level metadata in the associated repository, and whether the annotations were interoperable (e.g., host_disease = “Crohn's”). We also recorded whether manuscripts uploaded sample‐level metadata that matched sample identifiers in their corresponding repository locations. Tier 1 refers to studies with host disease status, age, and sex metadata fields (e.g., host_phenotype, host_age, host_sex). We focused on host disease, age, and sex because, for large‐scale human metagenomic databases, these three factors are often the most difficult yet most necessary factors to obtain and harmonize across many studies and samples [16]. Tier 2 studies at minimum included host disease status either as a metadata column or interpretable within the sample names (case1, control2, case3, etc.) (Figure S3). The justification for making Tier 2 solely reliant on health status is that age can often, although not always, be inferred as a categorical variable from study abstracts (e.g., “we sampled an adult cohort”), while disease status cannot be categorized at a study level unless the study lacked healthy controls. Moreover, within adults, age and sex contribute less to microbiome variation than health status in most large‐scale analyses [17]. Geography and antibiotic exposure were recorded for every study (Figure 2A) but kept out of the tier definition, due to geography frequently being a study‐wide attribute and few studies reporting antibiotic exposure. Tier 3 studies provided accession codes but lacked our defined host biological metadata of interest. Tier 4 studies lacked sample identifiers and annotations entirely or provided no accessible accession code in the manuscript.

caption.p: Human microbiome data reusability from 2012 to 2025. (A) Studies stacked by reusability tier (n = 2896); the inset shows the number of studies in which accession code, age, sex, disease, antibiotics (†), and geography are present. (B) Journal impact factor against the percentage of a journal's studies reaching Tier 1 or Tier 2; circle area is proportional to the number of studies from each journal with a Clarivate Journal Impact Factor. (C) Proportion of studies in Tiers 1–3 by year. Lines are multinomial‐logit trends with bootstrap 95% confidence bands; bubbles are observed proportions, sized by the number of studies published that year. (D) Proportion of studies that are Tier 4 (not reusable) or carry no accession code, plotted with the proportion whose repository records annotate disease, age, and sex per sample. (E) Sample‐level view of the dataset (about 720,000 samples); one block represents 5000 samples, colored by the tier of the study they belong to. (F) Sankey plot of manuscript‐level metadata deposition in a separate dataset of 2046 papers, recording whether authors uploaded custom metadata within the manuscript or as an associated link, and whether its sample identifiers matched the repository. p values in (C) and (D) are unadjusted; Holm‐adjusted values are given in Table S4. OR, odds ratio; RRR, relative risk ratio.

sec.p: Of the 2896 studies analyzed, 1157 (40.0%) cited a public sequence accession code, and 1069 (36.9%) led to usable sequence data (Tiers 1–3; Figure 2A). Across all 2,896 studies, 170 studies (5.9%) met Tier 1 criteria, 360 (12.4%) met Tier 2, 539 (18.6%) met Tier 3, and 1827 (63.1%) did not have accessible sequencing data and were thus labeled Tier 4 (Figure 2A). Across the four tiers, study sample sizes summed to 36,503 samples in Tier 1 (170 studies), 67,855 in Tier 2 (360 studies), 163,569 in Tier 3 (539 studies), and 452,170 in Tier 4 (1827 studies; calculated by Tiers 1–3 sample size averages). Thus, 615,739 (85.5%) of the 720,097 microbiome samples in our dataset are not reusable without additional external metadata files or author contact. See Data S1 for a full list of studies.

The number of microbiome papers published per year rose sharply across the study period (Figure 2A). However, the fraction of papers in each reusability class remained roughly constant (Figure S4), despite many calls to improve the situation. A multinomial logistic regression with publication year as the predictor and Tier 4 as the reference category found no significant temporal change in Tier 1 (relative risk ratio [RRR] = 1.047, p = 0.078) or Tier 2 (RRR = 1.003, p = 0.854), and a small but significant increase in Tier 3 (RRR = 1.045, p = 0.005; Holm‐adjusted p = 0.033) proportions (Figure 2C). A binary logistic regression showed that the proportion of studies lacking an accession code declined over the study period (odds ratio [OR] = 0.963 per year, p = 0.002; Holm‐adjusted p = 0.013), and the proportion that were not reusable at all fell slightly (Tier 4; OR = 0.970 per year, p = 0.012), although not after correction for multiple testing (Holm‐adjusted p = 0.075) (Figure 2D). Metadata completeness likewise failed to improve. Modeling the per‐year proportion of studies reporting each field by logistic regression on publication year (Figure 2D), host disease status (Tier 1–2; OR = 1.007, p = 0.658), host sex (OR = 1.037, p = 0.078), and host age (OR = 1.042, p = 0.035) showed no change after Holm correction across the 8 year‐effect tests (adjusted p ≥ 0.18). Deposition therefore improved modestly over the period, whereas per‐sample biological annotation did not. A natural‐spline year term fit no better than a linear one for any outcome (likelihood‐ratio p ≥ 0.20), and excluding the 888 studies from 2024 to 2025, whose deposits may have been incomplete when we curated them, strengthened rather than reversed these trends (Table S4).

Where studies were published was only weakly related to reusability. Modeling the probability that a study reached Tier 1 or Tier 2 as a function of journal impact factor, across the 53 journals with a Clarivate Journal Impact Factor and at least 10 studies represented, showed no association (OR = 1.08 per log10 unit, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.72–1.61, p = 0.711, n = 1474; Figure 2B, Figure S5, and Table S3). Studies in higher‐impact journals were, however, less likely to be non‐reusable (Tier 4; OR = 0.56 per log10 unit, 95% CI 0.39–0.80, p = 0.001; Figure S5B). Journal prestige was therefore associated with depositing sequence data, but not with annotating it (Figure S6A). Reusability tiers did differ by body site (χ 2 = 85.3, df = 21, p < 0.001; Figure S7C and Table S1), chiefly because studies sampling multiple body sites were over‐represented in Tier 4 and vaginal studies were under‐represented in Tier 1. Reusability tiers did not differ significantly across continents with at least 20 studies (χ 2 = 25.5, df = 18, p = 0.112; Figures S6B and S7A), and the year trend is unchanged when disease group, sequencing type, body site, and continent are added to the model or when standard errors are clustered by journal or disease group (Table S4).

By quantifying study sample size via ENA, we show the number of microbiome samples that are lost due to a lack of metadata (Figure 2E). Tier 1 and Tier 2 studies together contribute 104,358 of the 720,097 samples in our dataset, leaving approximately 615,739 samples (85.5%) that are lost due to a lack of structured metadata (Tier 4 study sample sizes calculated by taking the Tiers 1–3 average). From the Tier 1 and Tier 2 studies, we assembled a harmonized per‐sample ENA file with standardized disease, host age, and host sex annotations as a community resource of how proper metadata can facilitate large‐scale analysis (Data S2). Data S2 lists each of these samples once (115,015 samples); Table S5 and the Methods in the Supporting Information explain how it relates to the totals above. We harmonized disease fields by mapping them onto the Mondo Disease Ontology (MONDO) and its cross‐references to the Human Disease Ontology and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). Disease is recorded as a study‐level attribute, and each sample's case or control status is recorded separately, read only from that sample's own repository value; every distinct value was classified, and the basis for each sample's status is recorded in Data S2.

While AI tools will benefit the most from directly scraping repository metadata, authors often upload manuscript‐specific metadata as an external metadata file or embedded table. To assess the presence of these files, we also assessed manuscript metadata across a separate dataset of 2046 human microbiome studies (see Methods in the Supporting Information) and whether such metadata contained any identifiers that corresponded to sample identifiers in the associated repository accessions. Of the 1222 studies in this dataset that did deposit a public accession code, only 403 (33.0% of accession‐bearing studies; 19.7% of all 2046 studies) provided sample‐level metadata in their manuscripts, and, of those, 272 (67.5% of the 403, and 22.3% of accession‐bearing studies) used sample identifiers that actually matched the deposited sequence data (Figure 2F).

sec.title: DATA REUSABILITY IS NECESSARY FOR FUTURE LARGE‐SCALE MICROBIOME ANALYSES
sec.p: The disparity between uploading sequence data and actually annotating sequence data is especially exacerbated by the billions of taxpayer dollars spent globally on microbiome research each year [18], which inadvertently results in unusable data. Addressing this reusability crisis is therefore timely and important. Our tiered reusability framework provides the opportunity to assess and, more importantly, improve microbiome data reusability moving forward. Resources like Metalog and curatedMetagenomicData represent important curation efforts, but cannot scale to match the rate at which new data is being generated [13, 16]. Therefore, current incentive structures, including journal mandates, funding agency requirements, and community standards such as MIxS and STORMS, are insufficient or need to be revisited to drive the behavioral change required, including government mandates similar to those that drove DNA sequence accession in the first place [8, 9]. The Bermuda Principles, which still underpin much of the field's approach to data sharing, were designed for an era with much smaller and simpler datasets and do not address the rich metadata required for modern integrative analyses [11].

Thus, data reusability in microbiome research has essentially become a self‐reported honor system [9]. One critical step that we can strengthen is peer review, where reviewers and/or editors can open the accession and confirm that per‐sample metadata are present. This type of information is easily accessible with a single LLM prompt that will directly interact with ENA's API. Second, repository infrastructure must be updated to facilitate structured metadata entry. Current submission workflows at SRA, ENA, and DDBJ require minimal biological context, for valid reasons [7], but expanding required fields to include host health status, treatment group, basic demographics, body site, geographic location, and diet where it is relevant to the study design for biomedical microbiome papers would substantially increase the proportion of Tier 1 reusable data.

Finally, allowing NCBI and ENA submissions to be indexed and citable (i.e., showing up on authors' Google Scholar profiles) could add further incentive for authors to submit high‐quality metadata and provide authors with an additional avenue to receive citations for their work. Further, the development of community‐driven frameworks such as DRI tags would provide a standardized mechanism for data consumers to programmatically assess dataset reusability before investing effort in manual curation [11].

sec.title: TOWARD ON‐DEMAND SCALABLE MICROBIOME FOUNDATIONAL MODELS FOR AI‐LED DISCOVERIES
sec.p: The human microbiome field has generated an extraordinary wealth of public sequence data, but public availability does not equate to scientific utility. The lack of data, including complete metadata, prevents large‐scale computational reuse. Closing this gap is essential for the development of microbiome foundation models, AI‐driven drug discovery that leverages microbiome data, and the equitable reuse of publicly funded research. The steps we outline, including enforced metadata standards, improved repository infrastructure, AI‐assisted retroactive curation, and machine‐actionable reusability tags, provide a roadmap for transforming the microbiome field into a scalable AI‐ready resource. The rapid pace of data generation and persistent gaps in metadata completeness continue to constrain the scalability and performance of next‐generation microbiome AI tools.

sec.title: DATA AVAILABILITY STATEMENT
sec.p: The curated study‐level data, metadata classifications, and accession‐code records that support the findings of this study are available at https://github.com/samd1993/MMC along with our analysis scripts, including a standalone tool that takes an accession and reports which BHAM tier the deposit satisfies, so that authors, reviewers, and editors can check a submission against the criteria used here before it is published. The list of studies along with all the variables collected is available as Data S1, and the harmonized per‐sample metadata file is provided as Data S2. Data S2 keeps each study's disease as a study‐level column and records each sample's case or control status separately, from the sample's own repository value. An earlier build of this file attributed the study's disease to samples whose records reported no disease or did not name one; the version provided here corrects that error. Supplementary materials (methods, figures, tables, graphical abstract, slides, videos, Chinese translated version, and updated materials) may be found in the online DOI or iMeta Science http://www.imeta.science/.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The curated study‐level data, metadata classifications, and accession‐code records that support the findings of this study are available at https://github.com/samd1993/MMC along with our analysis scripts, including a standalone tool that takes an accession and reports which BHAM tier the deposit satisfies, so that authors, reviewers, and editors can check a submission against the criteria used here before it is published. The list of studies along with all the variables collected is available as Data S1, and the harmonized per‐sample metadata file is provided as Data S2. Data S2 keeps each study's disease as a study‐level column and records each sample's case or control status separately, from the sample's own repository value. An earlier build of this file attributed the study's disease to samples whose records reported no disease or did not name one; the version provided here corrects that error. Supplementary materials (methods, figures, tables, graphical abstract, slides, videos, Chinese translated version, and updated materials) may be found in the online DOI or iMeta Science http://www.imeta.science/.
